newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK retail sales to rebound in January.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK retail sales to rebound in January.

text.p: British retail sales data look set to show domestic demand has lost momentum since the feverish activity seen in the autumn months, but the strong underlying trend will remain intact, analysts said.

The data, due on Wednesday, are forecast to show a 0.2 percent rise on the month compared with December's surprise 0.8 percent fall. But the year-on-year rate of growth is expected to rise to 3.8 percent compared with 2.9 percent in December.
Kevin Gardiner, senior economist at Morgan Stanley, said even if the monthly figure is low, the underlying picture is one of robust growth with more strength to come.

"The fundamentals are right for domestic demand to stay robust. Real disposable income is growing at around 3.0 percent per annum, there are more people in work and consumers' balance sheets are getting stronger. Everything is clicking into place."

Gardiner forecasts a 0.5 percent rise in sales in January, well above the consensus. But economists said monthly figures covering December and January are typically very erratic and more emphasis should be placed on longer-term measures.

"The difficulty of adjusting for seasonal factors around the erratic Christmas and New Year period suggests that more attention should be paid to the underlying trend," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders.
He forecasts a 0.2 percent rise on the month but, "even with this outcome, the three-month-on-three-month change would stand at 0.7 percent, an annualised rate of 2.7 percent".
Surveys from the Confederation of British Industry and British Retail Consortium reported high street activity only partly bounced back after December's dismal pre-Christmas trading period.
But January retail prices figures showed record price discounting in clothing, footwear and household goods, suggesting sales may be strong in these key sectors.
The figures will be poured over by Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George who are at loggerheads over the need for an interest rate raise.

Last week, Clarke said that while the economy was growing steadily, there was no sign activity had accelerated since Christmas. The Bank, however, believes there is a risk domestic demand will pick up pace strongly.
"A soft number will play into the hands of the Chancellor and the currency is already doing that," said Kevin Adams, analyst at BZW.
"It would mean things are nicely poised for him, but it could present a new Chancellor with problems in the second half of the year."

The pound has appreciated by around 15 percent on a trade- weighted basis since the summer. Clarke has said its strength has had a deflationary effect on the economy. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7715
